Double Fine’s 99-player launch, Picardo blames politics for Starfleet Academy, Xbox’s AI post and more | The Reef Daily 
https://t.co/tqS7NvCTX4

Tim Schafer at the 2018 GDC IGF Awards. Photo: Official GDC, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0 (cropped)

Double Fine’s new game, Thank You, Bus Driver, peaked at 99 players on Steam, and Kneon thinks the studio has bigger problems than its failed union drive. Also on the list: an Xbox manager who said everybody in games uses AI and then deleted his account, Robert Picardo’s newest reason Starfleet Academy got canceled and Taika Waititi’s Star Wars movie going on ice. Further down, the Halo remakes that reportedly never happened, Modern Warfare 4’s early reviews and the newest Clownfish TV podcast episodes.

New Clownfish TV episodes

How many people are playing Double Fine’s Thank You, Bus Driver?

Almost nobody. The game peaked at 99 players at once on Steam, according to the report Kneon reads, and by the end of the recording only 16 people were playing. For comparison, he points out that Concord had about 700. Less than a day earlier came word that Day of the Tentacle Remastered and Full Throttle Remastered are leaving Game Pass. Double Fine’s games had stayed on the service since the studio joined Xbox in 2019.

Then Kotaku piled on. Its report says a majority of eligible Double Fine employees filed for a union with the National Labor Relations Board earlier this year and withdrew the petition two weeks later. When 23 people were laid off soon after, Kotaku reports, all eight organizers who signed it were among them. Tim Schafer told Kotaku that “in general, I’m pro-union.”

Kneon’s read is simpler. Any indie developer could put a game on Steam and beat 21 players, he says, and a studio in that spot has to make games people will pay for first.

Did an Xbox manager really say everyone uses AI?

Yes, and then he deleted his X account. An Xbox business strategy manager posted that Microsoft uses AI “just as all companies do in 2026” and that developers who won’t use it shouldn’t be in the business. He also wrote, “I’m happy to take the hit if it means hundreds can stop pretending that they’re not using AI.” He deleted the account after the replies piled up, sources told PC Gamer.

Kneon agrees with him. Refusing AI now is like doing long division while everybody else uses a calculator, he says, and Microsoft spends too much on Copilot to keep it out of its games.

The episode also covers a report, built on anonymous sources, that more Xbox layoffs are planned for October, November and January. The same report puts Microsoft’s internal estimate for its next console, Project Helix, at $1,200 to $1,800 unless Microsoft subsidizes it. And some Xbox owners say Microsoft emailed them about trading their consoles in at Best Buy for up to $375.

Why does Robert Picardo say Starfleet Academy was canceled?

Politics, this time. Picardo said “the present political moment in our culture” made Star Trek’s core values “out of fashion temporarily.” Fandom Pulse counts that as his fourth explanation since Paramount+ announced on March 24 that the show would end after Season 2. The earlier ones blamed a lack of ads, Paramount’s new owners, Elon Musk and Stephen Miller.

Fandom Pulse also pulled the numbers. None of the first 10 episodes made Nielsen’s weekly streaming top 10, and by June the show had an 85% critics score on Rotten Tomatoes next to a 52% audience score.

Kneon has loved Star Trek: The Next Generation since he was about 10, and he says the show just wasn’t good. He calls it “a CW show in space.” Even Enterprise star Dominic Keating said on his own podcast, with Picardo sitting across from him, that it was “a bit CW in space.”

Is Taika Waititi’s Star Wars movie canceled?

On ice, in his words. Waititi told Inverse, while promoting Klara and the Sun, “we’re going to actually put it on ice and we’re working on a different thing altogether.” Kneon guesses Rian Johnson’s long-promised Star Wars trilogy is dead too.

The hosts also get into artist Frank Cho’s claim, made in a podcast interview at New York Comic Con, that he has been banned from Marvel for three years. “I pissed off Kathleen Kennedy and she demanded Marvel ban me,” Cho said. He says it started with joke Star Wars sketch covers he drew as convention commissions, and that Kennedy ended the whole Star Wars sketch cover program over them. Bleeding Cool, which reported the interview, couldn’t find new Marvel work from Cho after 2022.

The hosts expect a lot more stories like this now that Kennedy is gone from Lucasfilm. Somebody, they figure, will write the tell-all.

PANEL 3 — BACK VIEW
Full-body rear view showing the back of the hairstyle, clothing construction, seams, fabric, silhouette, and footwear.

A high-resolution close-up of the character's face, showing realistic skin texture, natural pores, eyes, eyebrows, nose, lips, and hairstyle.

PANEL 5 — EYES CLOSE-UP
A detailed close-up of the character's eyes and eyebrows, preserving the exact eye shape, eye color, and surrounding facial features.

PANEL 6 — LIPS & FACIAL DETAILS
A close-up of the lips and lower facial area. For male characters, retain the exact beard, mustache, and facial hair if present. For female characters, preserve the natural lip shape and makeup shown in the reference.

PANEL 7 — OUTFIT DETAILS
Show close-up views of the most important clothing details, such as collars, buttons, embroidery, stitching, lace, sequins, decorative patterns, pockets, or garment construction.

PANEL 8 — ACCESSORIES & FOOTWEAR
Show the actual accessories and shoes from the reference image. If accessories are absent, use additional relevant outfit-detail shots instead.

PANEL 9 — FABRIC & MATERIAL TEXTURE
Show a macro-level detail of the actual clothing material, including realistic weave, folds, stitching, embroidery, shine, transparency, or surface texture as applicable.

COMPOSITION & CAMERA CONSISTENCY

Keep the same character identity across every panel.
Maintain consistent body proportions and physical appearance.
Use realistic full-body photography with correct anatomy.
Keep front, side, and back views anatomically consistent.
Use the same neutral grey studio environment throughout.
Use soft, professional studio lighting and natural shadows.
Maintain realistic skin texture and highly detailed clothing materials.
Ensure the full body, head, hands, legs, and shoes are not accidentally cropped in the three main views.

Make the composition look like a luxury fashion brand's professional character reference board.

PHOTOREALISM & QUALITY LOCK

Ultra-photorealistic photography, realistic skin pores, natural facial details, authentic fabric physics, precise garment construction, realistic hands, correct anatomy, sharp focus, premium studio photography, cinematic contrast, refined neutral color grading, exceptional fine detail.

Avoid plastic skin, artificial facial features, excessive beauty retouching, cartoon rendering, duplicated body parts, inconsistent faces, distorted hands, incorrect clothing, random accessories, altered colors, inconsistent hairstyles, and different identities between panels.

RESOLUTION LOCK

Generate the final image in the highest available resolution with a 16:9 aspect ratio. Preserve fine facial details, realistic fabric texture, sharp panel separation, and professional lookbook quality.

RESOLUTION LOCK: Generate final images in 16K resolution — 15360 × 8640 pixels (≈132.7 million pixels), 16:9 aspect ratio.

If the tool cannot produce native 16K output, generate at its highest supported resolution and upscale afterward without changing the character's identity or outfit.

FINAL INSTRUCTION

The uploaded reference image is the single source of truth for the character's identity, appearance, outfit, and styling.

Create ONE complete, premium, multi-panel professional character sheet featuring the exact same person in front, side, and back views, together with facial close-ups and outfit-detail photography.

Do not generate multiple unrelated characters. Do not create a new face. Do not change the original outfit.

FINAL RESULT: A cohesive, photorealistic, luxury fashion character reference sheet suitable for AI image generation, image-to-video workflows, cinematic filmmaking, fashion campaigns, and consistent character production.

Multi-objective protein optimization via modular diffusion steering

1 MODS is a modular framework that turns multi-objective protein design into inference-time steering of a fixed pretrained diffusion model, aiming to recover diverse Pareto tradeoffs under tight experimental-style budgets (few batched rounds).

2 Key idea: for each candidate proposal, MODS samples (a) augmented Chebyshev scalarization weights and (b) one member from a surrogate ensemble, combining them into a single scalar reward used for steering. Weight sampling explores different objective preferences; ensemble-member sampling explores predictive uncertainty.

3 The scalarization uses an augmented Chebyshev form: it emphasizes improving the worst-performing (weighted) objective while still rewarding progress on the others, helping recover tradeoffs on non-convex Pareto fronts where simple weighted sums can fail.

4 MODS separates “what to optimize” (multi-objective acquisition via scalar rewards) from “how to generate” (diffusion model + steering method). This makes the approach plug-and-play with different diffusion priors and compatible steering procedures.

5 Optimization loop: start with an initial evaluated set (100 sequences), then iterate 8 rounds of batched acquisition (100 sequences/round). After each round, MODS retrains only the fitness surrogate ensemble on accumulated observations, and reuses the same pretrained diffusion generator (no generator fine-tuning).

6 Implementations tested: two diffusion priors (MDLM masked diffusion LM; D3PM discrete diffusion) and two steering procedures (Classifier Guidance, CG; Decoupled Annealing Posterior Sampling, DAPS). Main comparisons focus on DAPS because it performed best across tasks.

7 Evaluation spans six assay-derived oracle benchmarks (5 two-objective tasks: GB1, ERBIN-PDZ1, NHERF3-PDZ2, KRAS, Src; 1 three-objective task: NHERF3-PDZ1). Oracles are CNN ensembles trained on experimental assay datasets with a distance-based penalty to discourage overconfident extrapolation far from labeled mutational neighborhoods.

8 Results: across all tasks, MODS improves substantially over unsteered sampling from the same diffusion model, and is competitive or best versus iterative baselines (ARLM+DPO, LaMBO-2, SAGE-Prot). In Table 1, MODS achieves the top mean final hypervolume on 5/6 tasks with D3PM+DAPS, and is close to the best baseline on Src with MDLM+DAPS.

9 Practical insight: steering strength matters. Too-weak regularization (oversteering away from the diffusion prior) can hurt on some tasks, consistent with reliance on less reliable surrogate predictions; the optimal setting depends jointly on task, diffusion prior, and steering procedure.

I think that two things will prove to be true at once.

1) Anthropic and OpenAI will prove to have very weak business economics under the surface. Come 2027/28, the ROI will simply not be there in large-enough fashion. There will be tons of demand for AI, but endless competition from lack of a substantial-enough barrier to entry will mean a race to the bottom in prices, even if they have great models/products. Google, Meta, everything in the realm of open source, Chinese models, and anyone else under the sun who brings a model forward will compete for use. OpenAI and Anthropic won't be able to prop up the amount of spend inherent in their businesses because of falling prices from competition.

2) Even with bad economics, OpenAI and Anthropic's products will remain very important to the USA and others. Being among the most advanced models means that there are certain things that their models will be best for. At least some advanced use-cases will likely show preference towards these models, and may even label them as necessary.

My tinfoil hat tells me that these businesses will IPO and, soon after, their profitability will show cracks. We will see a lot of red in the markets that will serve as an opportunity for buying because ultimately it will not disrupt the momentum of AI in general. Many stocks will crash, including the hyperscalers, and a year later we will be talking about how much of an overreaction it was. Kind of like the tarrif selloff of April 2025.

When OpenAI and Anthropic's stocks eventually fall, other large companies who can benefit by incorporating/utilizing their models, and who can support their continued development with their other cash flow generative business segments, will acquire them. $AAPL, $AMZN , and $MSFT come to mind as possibilities. Once all of that is done and behind us, the market will need to find another wall of worry to climb. And climb it will.
